\chapter{A While, a Way, a Thing}
\label{ch:manera-y-asunto}
\hlchaptermodality{331}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say el rato, la manera, el modo, la cosa and el asunto, and say which noun has been hiding inside como since chapter three.}

Complete ES-C331-asunto: cut a rato out of el tiempo, choose between manera and modo, and go from any cosa to the asunto it becomes.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el rato]{el rato — a while, snatched}

\label{lesson:ES-C331-rato}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{life}, then \emph{a time}. (\emph{La vida}; \emph{la vez}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el tiempo — the wider word this one cuts a piece out of.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{RA-to}, two beats with the weight on the first. The initial \emph{r} at the start of a word is rolled, not tapped — hold it for a moment. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el rato} — \textquotedblleft{}a while,\textquotedblright{} a short stretch of time.

The likeliest source is Latin \textbf{raptus}, \emph{a snatching}, from the verb \textbf{rapere}, \emph{to seize or carry off}. A \emph{rato} is a piece of time grabbed out of the flow — which is exactly the feeling of the English phrase \emph{a snatch of time}.

That gives you a third word for time, and the three do different jobs. \textbf{El tiempo} is time as substance. \textbf{La vez} is a countable occasion. \textbf{El rato} is a \emph{duration}, short and vague: \emph{un rato} is anywhere from a few minutes to most of an afternoon, and its vagueness is the point.

English inherited \emph{rapere} in a set of words that all still bite. Something \textbf{rapid} carries you off. A \textbf{raptor} is a bird that seizes. To be \textbf{rapt} is to be carried away by attention, and \textbf{rapture} is that state at full strength — a mind seized and taken. To \textbf{ravish} is the same verb through French.

Notice how many of them describe being taken against your will and how many describe delight. The root did not choose; it only ever meant \emph{seized}, and speakers decided each time whether being seized was good.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
The first of five words for the \emph{manner} and \emph{matter} of things — how something is done, and what it is about.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{un rato}
  \item \emph{el rato}
  \item \emph{un rato más}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{rapere} mean? (To seize, to carry off.) And which word means time as a substance rather than a stretch? (\emph{El tiempo}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la manera]{la manera — a way of doing is a way of handling}

\label{lesson:ES-C331-manera}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a time}, then \emph{a while}. (\emph{La vez}; \emph{el rato}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la mano — the word this one is built out of.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ma-NE-ra}, three beats with the weight in the middle. The \emph{r} is a single light tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la manera} — \textquotedblleft{}the way,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the manner.\textquotedblright{}

The first three letters give it away: \textbf{man-}. Latin \textbf{manus} was \emph{a hand}, and you met it as Spanish \textbf{la mano} long ago.

From \emph{manus} Latin built \textbf{manuārius}, \emph{belonging to the hand}, and the feminine of that became \textbf{manera}. So a \emph{way of doing something} is, at root, a \textbf{way of handling} it. English says the same thing without noticing — \emph{handling a situation}, \emph{a heavy-handed approach}, \emph{getting a handle on it}.

English \textbf{manner} is the same word, arriving through French \emph{manière}, and the whole family is unusually easy to spot because the hand stayed visible:

\textbf{Manual} work is hand work, and a \emph{manual} is a handbook. \textbf{Manufacture} is \emph{manu factum}, made by hand — a word coined before factories existed, which now names the opposite of handmade. A \textbf{manuscript} is \emph{manu scriptum}, written by hand. To \textbf{manage} is to handle, originally to handle a horse. To \textbf{maintain} is \emph{manū tenēre}, to hold in the hand. To \textbf{manipulate} is to work with the hands. And a \textbf{manoeuvre} is \emph{manū operāre}, to work by hand.

Spanish also has \textbf{de manera que}, \emph{in such a way that}, and \textbf{de ninguna manera}, \emph{in no way at all}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Two of five. \emph{La mano} has been in your vocabulary for hundreds of lessons; it turns out to have been holding this word.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la manera}
  \item \emph{de esta manera}
  \item \emph{de otra manera}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which body part is inside \emph{manera}? (\emph{La mano} — the hand.) And what does \emph{manufacture} mean word for word? (Made by hand.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el modo]{el modo — the word that has been inside \emph{cómo} since chapter three}

\label{lesson:ES-C331-modo}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{a while}, then \emph{the way}. (\emph{El rato}; \emph{la manera}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item cómo — the question word this noun is hiding inside.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{MO-do}, two beats, the weight on the first. Both \emph{o} sounds are short and rounded, and the \emph{d} between vowels is soft. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el modo} — \textquotedblleft{}the way,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the manner,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the mode.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{modus} meant \emph{a measure, a limit, a due amount}. Not a way of doing in the abstract, but the \textbf{size} of a thing — how much of it there should be.

That original sense explains a whole shelf of English words that otherwise look unrelated. To be \textbf{modest} is to keep to your measure. To \textbf{moderate} is to hold something to its measure. A \textbf{modicum} is a small measure. To \textbf{modify} is to change a measure. A \textbf{module} is a small measure used as a unit, and a \textbf{model} is a small measure of a large thing. Even \textbf{commodity} is \emph{com- modus}, something of the right measure — convenient, fitting.

\textbf{Modern} is the strangest of them: Late Latin \textbf{modo} meant \emph{only recently} — a \emph{measure} of time close to now — and \emph{modernus} was built on it.

Now the payoff that has been waiting since chapter three. Spanish \textbf{cómo} comes from Latin \textbf{quōmodo}, which is \textbf{quō} (\emph{in what}) plus \textbf{modo} (\emph{measure}) — \emph{in what measure? in what manner?} Every time you have asked \emph{¿cómo estás?} you have been asking \emph{in what manner are you?} and this noun was the second half of it.

\emph{Modo} and \emph{manera} overlap almost completely. \textbf{De todos modos} — \emph{at all events, anyway} — is one you will hear constantly.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Three of five. Two words for \emph{way}, and one of them was inside the first question you ever learned to ask.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el modo}
  \item \emph{de este modo}
  \item \emph{de todos modos}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{modus} mean? (A measure, a limit.) And which two Latin pieces make Spanish \emph{cómo}? (\emph{Quō} and \emph{modo} — in what measure.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la cosa]{la cosa — a thing that started out as a court case}

\label{lesson:ES-C331-cosa}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the way}, then \emph{the mode}. (\emph{La manera}; \emph{el modo}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item nada — the word that answers this one when there is no thing at all.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{CO-sa}, two beats with the weight on the first. The \emph{c} before \emph{o} is a hard \emph{k}, and the \emph{s} is crisp and unvoiced. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la cosa} — \textquotedblleft{}the thing.\textquotedblright{}

The most ordinary noun in the language has one of the strangest histories.

Latin \textbf{causa} meant \emph{a cause}, and more specifically \textbf{a legal case} — the matter being argued in a court. Roman lawyers said \emph{causa} constantly: \emph{the matter at hand, the business under discussion}.

Then the drift. \emph{The matter at hand} generalised to \emph{the matter}, and \emph{the matter} generalised to \emph{the thing}. By Vulgar Latin, \emph{causa} had stopped being legal and become the all-purpose word for anything at all. Spanish got \textbf{cosa}; French got \textbf{chose} by the same road, from the same word, at the same time.

But Spanish also has \textbf{la causa}, meaning \emph{the cause}. That is not the same inheritance — it is the Latin word borrowed back later, straight from books, with its original meaning intact. Spanish therefore owns \emph{causa} twice: once worn down by mouths into \emph{cosa}, and once carried in by scholars unchanged. Linguists call that pair a \textbf{doublet}.

English never inherited the drifted form, only the learned one, so the courtroom sense stayed put: a \textbf{cause}, to \textbf{accuse}, to \textbf{excuse}, and \textbf{because}, which is \emph{by cause}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four of five. With \emph{cosa} you can talk about something whose name you do not know, which is one of the most useful things a beginner can do.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la cosa}
  \item \emph{otra cosa}
  \item \emph{una cosa más}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{causa} mean? (A cause, and a legal case.) And which French word took the identical road? (\emph{Chose}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el asunto]{el asunto — a matter is a thing taken up}

\label{lesson:ES-C331-asunto}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{the mode}, then \emph{the thing}. (\emph{El modo}; \emph{la cosa}.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la cosa — the wider word this one narrows.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{a-SUN-to}, three beats with the weight in the middle. The \emph{s} is crisp, and the \emph{n} before \emph{t} is made with the tongue already at the teeth. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el asunto} — \textquotedblleft{}the matter,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the affair,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}the business at hand.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{sūmere} meant \emph{to take}. Add \textbf{ad-} and you get \textbf{assūmere}, \emph{to take up}, whose past participle is \textbf{assūmptus} — \emph{taken up}. Spanish smoothed the \emph{mp} away and got \textbf{asunto}.

So an \emph{asunto} is, precisely, \textbf{a matter that has been taken up}. Somebody raised it; now it is somebody's business. That is a sharper word than \emph{cosa}, which is any thing at all. A \emph{cosa} can sit there being a thing. An \emph{asunto} is a thing that has become somebody's business.

English kept \emph{sūmere} busy. To \textbf{assume} is to take something up — either a duty you take on, or a premise you take as given. An \textbf{assumption} is either. To \textbf{resume} is to take up again. To \textbf{consume} is to take completely. To \textbf{presume} is to take beforehand. To be \textbf{sumptuous} is to involve a great taking, which is why it means lavish. And \textbf{sumptuary} laws were rules limiting how much people could spend.

If you have an email in Spanish, the subject line is labelled \textbf{asunto} — the matter this message takes up.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five words for how and what: \emph{el rato}, \emph{la manera}, \emph{el modo}, \emph{la cosa}, \emph{el asunto}. Between them, you can point at any topic without naming it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el asunto}
  \item \emph{otro asunto}
  \item \emph{un asunto más}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did Latin \emph{sūmere} mean? (To take.) And what is an \emph{asunto}, taken literally? (A matter taken up.)
\end{tcolorbox}
